# Claudinite — where content goes (pack routing)

Each pack states what it owns and what it does not. When a rule, doc, skill or check could live in more than one, this table decides it — and "no pack fits" means a new pack or the project's own `local_packs/`, never the baseline by default.

| Pack | Belongs | Does not belong |
|---|---|---|
| `barriers` | directed folder-access graph rules — which directories may never reference which, plus the exceptions each rule allows | where a file should live or naming conventions — that is basics file-placement, not an access barrier |
| `basics` | cross-project working discipline, issue-branch-PR lifecycle, repo hygiene, doc/reference integrity and the baseline engineering, testing and debugging skills | technology-specific content — its own tech pack; GitHub Actions workflow or platform behaviour — github-actions; git procedure — git-github |
| `executable-requirements` | running a numbered spec as tests: dev/requirements layout, requirement ids, kinds, coverage and gallery gates, determinism rules | doc-first judgment, owner-owned expecteds and honest-gap tracking — spec-driven-product; general test practice — basics writing-tests |
| `git-github` | git and GitHub procedure: commit layering, branch and merge mechanics, squash-merge recovery, PR and merge-to-main commands | the issue-branch-PR lifecycle rules themselves — basics; workflow YAML and Actions runtime behaviour — github-actions |
| `github-actions` | workflow YAML and Actions runner platform behaviour: triggers, secrets, permissions, scheduling, artifacts, reusable workflows and their pitfalls | git and GitHub command procedure — git-github; release pipeline content for one product — its release pack |
| `grow_with_claudinite` | rules and tasks for capturing lessons into local packs — extraction, dedup, conversation logs, skill-usage folding | repo housekeeping of issues, PRs and branches — that is tidy-repo; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `html` | hand-authored HTML markup gotchas — element nesting, injected content placement, live browser verification of a page | javascript runtime APIs — web-speech; map widgets — leaflet; npm and dependency policy — node |
| `product-wiki` | agent-maintained market, user and competitor research wikis — cited pages, growth logs, the reviewed product-requirements sink | how the product is built or specced — that is spec-driven-product; requirement proofs are executable-requirements |
| `spec-driven-product` | playbook for shipping a small end-user product from an executable spec — leaf claims, owner-owned expecteds, green-main releases | the requirements file format and coverage gates — that is executable-requirements; research wikis are product-wiki |
| `tidy-repo` | housekeeping of open issues, pull requests and branches in one repo — triage verdicts, standing trackers, assess-vs-act policy | extracting lessons into packs — that is grow_with_claudinite; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `edfringe` (local) | EdFringeNow's own working rules — its build steps, shell scripts, and repo layout conventions | the edfringe.com scrape and the data layer it produces — those are edfringe-data |
| `edfringe-data` (local) | the edfringe.com scrape and the committed data layer it produces — external-API and wire-format knowledge | UI work and general repo working rules — those are edfringe |

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).

1	# Growth — extract lessons (per repo)
2	
3	The growth lifecycle's capture stage, over **both** lesson sources in one run: the window's repo activity
4	(commits, merged PRs, issue discussion) and the conversation logs captured from working sessions. Each
5	durable, reusable lesson is folded into the repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/` — the
6	normalized capture surface) at the repo's own level, without straining to generalize it. The run lands its
7	edits through a single PR **delivered to land** (on the default delivery settings it merges once the repo's
8	checks pass, with no human review — daily capture never piles up as review requests); finding nothing to add
9	on a given run is a perfectly good outcome.
10	
11	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding
12	scope**: it names which halves are live, the substantive commit shas and the PRs/issues touched in the
13	window, and whether the retention prune is due. That is the work; do not widen it.
14	
15	> This is the **unattended daily** capture. It writes only the repo's *own* local packs, so — **unlike** an
16	> owner-requested, in-session retrospective (which delivers a PR for a human to review) — it opens a PR and
17	> **delivers it to land** (the shared procedure under *Output* below; on the default settings GitHub lands it
18	> once the repo's checks pass). The shared canon stays human-gated — lifting anything up into it is the
19	> central promote task's job (canon-side), and that PR waits for the owner.
20	
21	## Conventions used in this doc
22	
23	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
24	- **Access split — local git for repo content, MCP for the issue/PR API.** The repo's own content is plain
25	  **local git** in the checkout: the commits, the `conversation-logs` branch and its files
26	  (`git fetch`/`show`/`rm`/`push`), and staging the lesson edits onto a branch. Reading issue/PR activity,
27	  opening the PR and delivering it, posting the exchange summaries and the tracking-issue log go
28	  through the session's **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub
29	  access — the shell reaches only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so
30	  never reach for `gh`/`curl` or a cross-repo clone.
31	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in
32	  [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) — everything
33	  under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename
34	  window), the repo's own packs; never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
35	
36	## The run — two source skills, then the upgrade pass
37	
38	The **method** for each source lives in its skill; this worker only frames the run around them. Don't
39	re-derive any of it here.
40	
41	1. **Activity half — the [extract-from-activity](../../skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) skill**, over
42	   exactly the commits, merged PRs and issues named in Context. **Skip this half entirely when Context says
43	   the activity half is not in scope** (a quiet repo whose only reason to run was the retention prune).
44	2. **Conversation half — the [extract-from-conversations](../../skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
45	   skill**, over the repo's captured logs. `git fetch origin conversation-logs`, then list its files
46	   (`git ls-tree --name-only origin/conversation-logs`); no branch, or no `*.jsonl`, and this half is done.
47	   Give each log captured in the recent window a **fresh pass** (its filename carries the capture stamp;
48	   corpus dedup makes an overlapping re-read harmless, so err toward re-reading the last several days), and
49	   post the skill's provenance summary for each rule that actually lands.
50	3. **Retention prune**, when Context says it is due. Read `retention_days` from this repo's
51	   `.claudinite-checks.json` (the grow_with_claudinite entry's `config.retention_days`) — unset means this
52	   step is skipped entirely (capture-only adoption). For each log whose filename stamp is older than
53	   `retention_days` days: give it the **final hindsight pass** the skill describes (anything it still yields
54	   lands like any other keeper), then `git rm` it on the `conversation-logs` branch and push (commit message
55	   ending `[skip ci]`). The branch is never merged and its history is never rewritten — plain add/remove
56	   commits only. This push to the non-default logs branch is outside the outcome taxonomy (DESIGN §1).
57	4. **Upgrade pass — the [prose-to-checks](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) skill, over what *this run*
58	   just wrote.** Both halves route down the local promotion ladder as they go, but a lesson written as prose
59	   under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides. So before opening the PR, take the prose
60	   this run added and ask the skill's questions of it: does it clear the working-rule gate, and does it
61	   constrain a static signature a check could observe? If yes, convert it now — author the rule module,
62	   register it in its pack's `pack.mjs`, prove it with a **see-it-fail** fixture, and apply the deletion
63	   test to the prose the check now stands beside. **Scope is this run's own additions only** — the standing
64	   prose backlog is the weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)'s job, and widening
65	   into it here would duplicate that task's work under an auto-merging PR.
66	
67	If an edit touches something a test reads (a doc constant, a code path), run the repo's offline test suite
68	and keep it green before opening the PR.
69	
70	## Output: one PR, delivered to land
71	
72	If the run found at least one genuinely new lesson, it lands **all** of it — both halves, plus any check the
73	upgrade pass produced — through a **single PR**: one commit for the whole run on a per-run-unique branch, not
74	one per lesson and not one per half. Open the PR (title `Claudinite growth: extract lessons`, its commit
75	referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes), then **deliver it by the shared
76	procedure — [deliver-pr.md](../../../../engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md)**. That procedure — never this file —
77	owns every landing nuance: it reads this repo's `maintenance.delivery` (a `review` repo's PR waits for the
78	owner — still a delivered outcome), arms auto-merge where the repo allows it, and licenses the hand merge
79	when the arm is rejected `clean status` (a base branch that requires nothing — GitHub never auto-merges
80	there). Do not assume this run's PR merges unreviewed: that is the repo's setting, not this task's. On the
81	default settings it squash-merges once the repo's checks pass, so daily lesson-capture never floods review
82	requests while every change still gets a PR trail and a CI gate. This writes only the repo's *own* local
83	packs (not the shared canon). A run that finds nothing and opens nothing is fine — and common.
84	
85	A new check must ship green — see it fail on a violating fixture, pass on a clean one — so CI stays green and
86	the PR can merge; a check that can't be made confident lands its lesson as prose instead, never a broken check.
87	
88	## Tracking: log each run under the task's own issue
89	
90	The task's standing log is the issue titled exactly, in this repo:
91	
92	> **Claudinite tracker: Growth Extract**
93	
94	Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle, and it
95	differs per repo). A run that finds no issue under the exact title just creates one (closed). **Never open,
96	close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning, only the log does. When a run adds a lesson,
97	converts one to a check, or prunes logs, log it as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue — so the issue
98	accumulates a scrollable history, each entry naming **what happened and where**. A run that changed nothing
99	logs nothing. (A repo that still carries a closed `Claudinite tracker: Conversation Extract` issue from when
100	the halves were two tasks keeps it as history — never post to it, never reopen it.)
101	
102	## Run on a capable model
103	
104	Deciding whether a lesson is genuinely new and durable — and deduping it against what's already documented —
105	is a **judgment call**, not mechanical extraction. A downgraded model adds noise or restates what's there,
106	and **on the default delivery no human reviews the PR before it lands** — CI gates correctness, not whether a
107	"lesson" earns its keep — so the capable-model requirement matters all the more. This task declares
108	`agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
109	
110	## What this task must never do
111	
112	- **Never touch the shared canon** — this task writes only the repo's *own* local packs under
113	  `.claudinite/local/packs/`; everything else under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mount, and lifting a
114	  lesson up into the canon is the central promote task's job.
115	- **Never widen past the Context window** — the halves it declares live, the substantive commits and the
116	  touched PRs/issues named there are the scope; do not re-decide it. That includes the upgrade pass: this
117	  run's own additions, never the standing backlog.
118	- **Never merge `conversation-logs`** anywhere, and never rewrite its history — plain add and remove commits only.
119	- **Never paste the conversation onto an issue** — not raw JSONL, not a rendered transcript, not the turns
120	  themselves. Each landed rule gets one ≤200-word summary of the exchange behind it, and nothing more.
121	- **Never delete a log younger than retention, and never delete anything while `retention_days` is unset** —
122	  deletion is the ack that both passes happened.
123	- **Don't add noise** — a duplicate or hallucinated "lesson" is worse than adding nothing, the more so when
124	  its PR usually lands with no human review to catch it.

   skill**, over the repo's captured logs. `git fetch origin conversation-logs`, then list its files

1	# Growth — extract lessons (per repo)
2	
3	The growth lifecycle's capture stage, over **both** lesson sources in one run: the window's repo activity
4	(commits, merged PRs, issue discussion) and the conversation logs captured from working sessions. Each
5	durable, reusable lesson is folded into the repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/` — the
6	normalized capture surface) at the repo's own level, without straining to generalize it. The run lands its
7	edits through a single PR **delivered to land** (on the default delivery settings it merges once the repo's
8	checks pass, with no human review — daily capture never piles up as review requests); finding nothing to add
9	on a given run is a perfectly good outcome.
10	
11	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding
12	scope**: it names which halves are live, the substantive commit shas and the PRs/issues touched in the
13	window, and whether the retention prune is due. That is the work; do not widen it.
14	
15	> This is the **unattended daily** capture. It writes only the repo's *own* local packs, so — **unlike** an
16	> owner-requested, in-session retrospective (which delivers a PR for a human to review) — it opens a PR and
17	> **delivers it to land** (the shared procedure under *Output* below; on the default settings GitHub lands it
18	> once the repo's checks pass). The shared canon stays human-gated — lifting anything up into it is the
19	> central promote task's job (canon-side), and that PR waits for the owner.
20	
21	## Conventions used in this doc
22	
23	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
24	- **Access split — local git for repo content, MCP for the issue/PR API.** The repo's own content is plain
25	  **local git** in the checkout: the commits, the `conversation-logs` branch and its files
26	  (`git fetch`/`show`/`rm`/`push`), and staging the lesson edits onto a branch. Reading issue/PR activity,
27	  opening the PR and delivering it, posting the exchange summaries and the tracking-issue log go
28	  through the session's **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub
29	  access — the shell reaches only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so
30	  never reach for `gh`/`curl` or a cross-repo clone.
31	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in
32	  [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) — everything
33	  under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename
34	  window), the repo's own packs; never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
35	
36	## The run — two source skills, then the upgrade pass
37	
38	The **method** for each source lives in its skill; this worker only frames the run around them. Don't
39	re-derive any of it here.
40	
41	1. **Activity half — the [extract-from-activity](../../skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) skill**, over
42	   exactly the commits, merged PRs and issues named in Context. **Skip this half entirely when Context says
43	   the activity half is not in scope** (a quiet repo whose only reason to run was the retention prune).
44	2. **Conversation half — the [extract-from-conversations](../../skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
45	   skill**, over the repo's captured logs. `git fetch origin conversation-logs`, then list its files
46	   (`git ls-tree --name-only origin/conversation-logs`); no branch, or no `*.jsonl`, and this half is done.
47	   Give each log captured in the recent window a **fresh pass** (its filename carries the capture stamp;
48	   corpus dedup makes an overlapping re-read harmless, so err toward re-reading the last several days), and
49	   post the skill's provenance summary for each rule that actually lands.
50	3. **Retention prune**, when Context says it is due. Read `retention_days` from this repo's
51	   `.claudinite-checks.json` (the grow_with_claudinite entry's `config.retention_days`) — unset means this
52	   step is skipped entirely (capture-only adoption). For each log whose filename stamp is older than
53	   `retention_days` days: give it the **final hindsight pass** the skill describes (anything it still yields
54	   lands like any other keeper), then `git rm` it on the `conversation-logs` branch and push (commit message
55	   ending `[skip ci]`). The branch is never merged and its history is never rewritten — plain add/remove
56	   commits only. This push to the non-default logs branch is outside the outcome taxonomy (DESIGN §1).
57	4. **Upgrade pass — the [prose-to-checks](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) skill, over what *this run*
58	   just wrote.** Both halves route down the local promotion ladder as they go, but a lesson written as prose
59	   under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides. So before opening the PR, take the prose
60	   this run added and ask the skill's questions of it: does it clear the working-rule gate, and does it
61	   constrain a static signature a check could observe? If yes, convert it now — author the rule module,
62	   register it in its pack's `pack.mjs`, prove it with a **see-it-fail** fixture, and apply the deletion
63	   test to the prose the check now stands beside. **Scope is this run's own additions only** — the standing
64	   prose backlog is the weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)'s job, and widening
65	   into it here would duplicate that task's work under an auto-merging PR.
66	
67	If an edit touches something a test reads (a doc constant, a code path), run the repo's offline test suite
68	and keep it green before opening the PR.
69	
70	## Output: one PR, delivered to land
71	
72	If the run found at least one genuinely new lesson, it lands **all** of it — both halves, plus any check the
73	upgrade pass produced — through a **single PR**: one commit for the whole run on a per-run-unique branch, not
74	one per lesson and not one per half. Open the PR (title `Claudinite growth: extract lessons`, its commit
75	referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes), then **deliver it by the shared
76	procedure — [deliver-pr.md](../../../../engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md)**. That procedure — never this file —
77	owns every landing nuance: it reads this repo's `maintenance.delivery` (a `review` repo's PR waits for the
78	owner — still a delivered outcome), arms auto-merge where the repo allows it, and licenses the hand merge
79	when the arm is rejected `clean status` (a base branch that requires nothing — GitHub never auto-merges
80	there). Do not assume this run's PR merges unreviewed: that is the repo's setting, not this task's. On the
81	default settings it squash-merges once the repo's checks pass, so daily lesson-capture never floods review
82	requests while every change still gets a PR trail and a CI gate. This writes only the repo's *own* local
83	packs (not the shared canon). A run that finds nothing and opens nothing is fine — and common.
84	
85	A new check must ship green — see it fail on a violating fixture, pass on a clean one — so CI stays green and
86	the PR can merge; a check that can't be made confident lands its lesson as prose instead, never a broken check.
87	
88	## Tracking: log each run under the task's own issue
89	
90	The task's standing log is the issue titled exactly, in this repo:
91	
92	> **Claudinite tracker: Growth Extract**
93	
94	Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle, and it
95	differs per repo). A run that finds no issue under the exact title just creates one (closed). **Never open,
96	close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning, only the log does. When a run adds a lesson,
97	converts one to a check, or prunes logs, log it as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue — so the issue
98	accumulates a scrollable history, each entry naming **what happened and where**. A run that changed nothing
99	logs nothing. (A repo that still carries a closed `Claudinite tracker: Conversation Extract` issue from when
100	the halves were two tasks keeps it as history — never post to it, never reopen it.)
101	
102	## Run on a capable model
103	
104	Deciding whether a lesson is genuinely new and durable — and deduping it against what's already documented —
105	is a **judgment call**, not mechanical extraction. A downgraded model adds noise or restates what's there,
106	and **on the default delivery no human reviews the PR before it lands** — CI gates correctness, not whether a
107	"lesson" earns its keep — so the capable-model requirement matters all the more. This task declares
108	`agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
109	
110	## What this task must never do
111	
112	- **Never touch the shared canon** — this task writes only the repo's *own* local packs under
113	  `.claudinite/local/packs/`; everything else under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mount, and lifting a
114	  lesson up into the canon is the central promote task's job.
115	- **Never widen past the Context window** — the halves it declares live, the substantive commits and the
116	  touched PRs/issues named there are the scope; do not re-decide it. That includes the upgrade pass: this
117	  run's own additions, never the standing backlog.
118	- **Never merge `conversation-logs`** anywhere, and never rewrite its history — plain add and remove commits only.
119	- **Never paste the conversation onto an issue** — not raw JSONL, not a rendered transcript, not the turns
120	  themselves. Each landed rule gets one ≤200-word summary of the exchange behind it, and nothing more.
121	- **Never delete a log younger than retention, and never delete anything while `retention_days` is unset** —
122	  deletion is the ack that both passes happened.
123	- **Don't add noise** — a duplicate or hallucinated "lesson" is worse than adding nothing, the more so when
124	  its PR usually lands with no human review to catch it.
125

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
11	
12	Your task's declared `expected_outcome` is a **ceiling, not a plan**:
13	
14	- **`open-pr`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
15	  applies to you.
16	- **`merged-pr`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
17	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
18	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
19	
20	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
21	
22	`.claudinite-checks.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
23	
24	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
25	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
26	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading `merged-pr`
27	  to open-pr is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
28	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
29	  materializing it is baselining's converge job, not yours.
30	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
31	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
32	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the dispatch issue.
33	
34	## 2. Arm auto-merge
35	
36	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
37	it once this repo's required checks pass.
38	
39	## 3. When the arm is rejected
40	
41	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
42	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
43	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
44	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
45	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
46	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
47	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
48	  PR's **head sha**:
49	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
50	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
51	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
52	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
53	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
54	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
55	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
56	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
57	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
58	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
59	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
60	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
61	    unseen check does not survive anything.
62	
63	## Never
64	
65	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
66	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
67	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
68	are always legal outcomes.

1	---
2	name: extract-from-activity
3	description: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from repo activity
7	
8	The **artifact** half of lesson extraction: mine what a window of work left behind — commits, the PRs
9	merged in it, the issue discussion around them — for durable, reusable lessons, and fold each into the
10	repo's **own local packs**. Its sibling [extract-from-conversations](../extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
11	mines the *dialogue*; this one never sees a conversation, only what the work committed.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives are shared with that sibling and stay canonical in
15	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't re-derive it. What follows is only
16	what reading *artifacts* adds.
17	
18	## Capture at the repo's own level
19	
20	Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or
21	mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear. Don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson
22	to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the
23	growth lifecycle's **promote** stage, done canon-side later over whatever merged here; here, just capture
24	it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.
25	
26	## Read the window — and read merged PRs properly
27	
28	Work only the window you were handed (a scheduled run gets it as binding scope in the dispatch issue's
29	Context; an owner's ask names it in words). Never widen it.
30	
31	1. **The commits** — full bodies, and the diff wherever a fix is non-obvious.
32	2. **The PRs merged in the window** — read these *first* and read them *whole*: the diff **and** the
33	   review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source, because it records what
34	   was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won. A verdict reached in review
35	   is a lesson already argued; the commit alone shows only the winner.
36	3. **The issue activity** it names — the comments changed on those numbers.
37	
38	## What artifacts signal — and what they don't
39	
40	The signals worth converting here are the ones an artifact can carry: a fix whose diff is small but whose
41	*reason* is not obvious from the code; a review comment that names a convention the author missed; a
42	revert or a follow-up fix that says the first shape was wrong; a PR that grew several rounds because its
43	approach was re-decided mid-flight.
44	
45	**An already-settled, already-enforced implementation choice is not a lesson.** If a check or a test
46	already pins the shape — which roots a CI sweep walks, which contract a construction must satisfy — and
47	all that is left to say is *why it looks like that*, that explanation belongs as a comment at the
48	implementation site, not as prose in a pack. A rule earns its place by steering a **future** decision or
49	catching a **repeatable** mistake, not by narrating a past one that is already locked in.
50	
51	Wall-time and dialogue friction (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a wait sat through) leave no trace
52	in a diff. Don't infer them from artifacts — that is the conversation sibling's territory, working from
53	logs that actually carry the timestamps.
54	
55	## Landing it
56	
57	Route each keeper down the ladder in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — check first,
58	then pack skill, prose last — into the local pack whose territory owns it. Write more checks and less
59	prose, and keep each addition terse and in the repo's own voice.
60	
61	A new check ships **green or not at all**: see it fail on a violating fixture and pass on a clean one. A
62	rule that cannot be made confident lands as prose instead — never as a broken check.
63	
64	Finding nothing is a perfectly good and common outcome; a duplicate or invented "lesson" is worse than
65	adding nothing.
66

1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first
94	
95	A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
96	retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
97	formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
98	landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.
99	
100	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
101	
102	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
103	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
104	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
105	
106	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
107	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
108	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
109	
110	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
111	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
112	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
113	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
114	silence it replaced.
115

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
29	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
30	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
31	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
32	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
33	
34	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
35	
36	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
37	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
38	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
39	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
40	
41	1. **A check** in that pack's rules — author the `.mjs`, list it on the pack's `pack.mjs`, ship it with a
42	   red-first fixture. Its failure message *is* the lesson.
43	2. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
44	3. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — only what neither of the above can carry.
45	
46	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
47	relocates it. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson warrants segregation, a new local pack is a
48	self-contained directory drop.
49	
50	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all.** A trap from misusing a specific API, class, or
51	library goes as a **comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where the next editor of
52	that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list. Co-locate it in a file's own header
53	comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a
54	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
55	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
56	
57	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
58	
59	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
60	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
61	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
62	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
63

===EDFRINGE RULES===
# EdFringeNow — project working rules

Lessons captured while working in this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
canon. Terse and concrete; read the matching one before working in that area.

## The owner asks in plain words — open the issue yourself, before the first commit

Work here arrives as a chat request ("Maybe we can just put a 'Show list/Show Map'
toggle selector just under the filter…"), never as a filed issue. The
`task-lifecycle` check still wants a commit on the branch to reference one, so
**open the issue as your first step and put `Closes #N` in the original commit
message** — write it from the owner's own words, since it is the only record of
what was asked.

Leaving it to the stop hook is the expensive path, and it is the path every
session took: 7 of the 12 sessions captured on 2026-07-29 declared the work done,
got blocked, and then paid create-issue + `git commit --amend` +
`git push --force-with-lease` + a second reply that added nothing (#134 33s,
#150 45s, #152 35s, #154 43s, #156 43s, #158 57s, #160 20s — ~4.6 min of pure
rework). Worse, by then the PR is already open, so the fix rewrites the commit
underneath it.

## A dispatched run still has to classify its trigger comment

The `comment-classification` check reads the last message addressed to you and
wants a `Comment class:` line in the reply to it. In a scheduled run that message
is the executor prompt ("Execute the Claudinite executor: …"), not anything the
owner wrote — but the check does not distinguish them, and it is BLOCKING at the
Stop hook. 19 of the sessions captured across 2026-07-29…07-31 were stopped by
exactly this finding, every one of them citing the dispatch prompt, and each paid
an extra closing reply to clear it (the two runs where the block lands at the end
and the cost is cleanly isolable: #183 115s, #160 121s).

So **close a dispatched run's final reply with an explicit `Comment class:` line
classifying the dispatch itself** — `process-change` for an executor/scheduled-task
prompt — instead of discovering the requirement at Stop. On a real owner comment
the classification is the substance; on a dispatch it is a formality, but it is
far cheaper paid up front than as a second reply.

## Read the PR's state, then merge — never loop on `enable_pr_auto_merge`

`mcp__github__enable_pr_auto_merge` only accepts a PR whose required checks are
still **pending**. This repo's `ci.yml` runs on `pull_request` and finishes in
well under a minute, so by the time an agent reaches the arming step the PR is
usually already `clean` and the call errors — *"already in clean status (all
checks passed) … you can merge directly."* That is not a failure to work around:
take it as the answer and call `mcp__github__merge_pull_request` with `SQUASH`.

The other refusal, *"in unstable status (required checks are failing)"*, is not a
verdict either — a check that is queued, or held at the Actions approval gate,
reads identically to one that failed. Re-read the PR
(`mcp__github__pull_request_read`) or the run list (`mcp__github__actions_list`)
to find out which, and never re-arm on a loop: PR #188 answered "unstable" and
then "clean" 27s later with nothing changed in between, and PR #182 answered
"unstable" three times across ~4 minutes before answering "clean".

The cost is measured. The 2026-08-01 baselining run spent ~350s of its 765s — 4
arm attempts, 9 `pull_request_read`s and 5 `ScheduleWakeup` polls — circling PR
#182's merge state, and still ended without merging it; the owner merged it by
hand the next evening. The same morning's conversation-extract run took its one
refusal as an answer and squash-merged 22s later. Check state first, merge
directly when it is clean, and arm auto-merge only while checks are genuinely
pending.

## Verifying UI changes visually (the `index.html` page and everything under `plan/`)

Visual verification of the pages **is** available in this sandbox. Don't skip it
or downgrade to "verified by logic review only" claiming no browser exists — a
browser is here, and a UI change isn't done until it has been looked at.

- Serve the repo and drive it with the preinstalled Chromium (or Playwright):
  `python3 -m http.server 8000`, then screenshot / click through
  `http://localhost:8000`. The app fetches `data/shows.json`, so it must be
  served over HTTP rather than opened as a file — and `localhost` bypasses the
  agent proxy, so the browser reaches the page even though external hosts need
  the proxy.
- **Launch Playwright with no `executablePath`, and import from `index.mjs`.**
  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers` is already exported in this
  sandbox, so `chromium.launch()` finds its browser on its own. Import the
  global build by its ESM entry —
  `import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'`
  (the sibling `index.js` is CJS, so a *named* import from it yields
  `undefined`) — or `$(npm root -g)/playwright/index.mjs` if the prefix moved.
  Path discovery and its sed-fix-up round-trips cost ~220s across five captured
  sessions, every one of them re-deriving the same two facts.
  `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium` is a **symlink** onto the version-pinned
  `chromium-<build>/chrome-linux/chrome`, so it is a valid `executablePath` if
  you ever need one — but you don't, and the build it points at moves with the
  image.
- **Never `npm i playwright` into the scratchpad to make the import resolve.**
  A bare `import { chromium } from 'playwright'` in a scratchpad script fails
  with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — the global install is not on the resolution
  path, and `NODE_PATH` does not apply to ESM, so exporting it changes nothing.
  The obvious next move is the wrong one: a fresh `npm i playwright` pulls a
  **newer** Playwright than the image's, which then hunts for a browser build
  the image does not ship (`chromium_headless_shell-1234` against the vendored
  `-1194`) and dies asking for `npx playwright install` — a download the
  sandbox cannot make. Three sessions on 2026-08-07 (#251, #258, #264) each
  took that detour and then backed out of it. Use the absolute path to the
  global build instead: it is the one matched to the vendored browsers.
- **Keep one browser driver script per session and re-point it.** Authoring a
  fresh throwaway Playwright script per screenshot cost 29 heredoc writes and
  ~7 minutes of wall clock across the captured sessions (one session alone: 16
  writes, 4.5 min). Write the driver once into the scratchpad, take the URL,
  selector and output path from `process.argv`, and re-run it — a re-run is
  seconds where a rewrite is 15–20s.
- To build a `/plan` favourites list for the render, a plain slug-per-line text
  file is accepted by the parser — pick shows spanning the statuses (and some
  same-day doubles) you want to eyeball.
- **Known-noisy console output from the served page.** A page driven off
  `python3 -m http.server` reliably logs a `favicon.ico` 404 (the repo ships
  none) and often `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` as the browser tears down. Neither
  is an application error — filter both out of a smoke script's error assertion
  so that a red run means something, rather than sending you chasing a phantom
  404 through extra browser runs.
- To match edfringe.com's live styling (e.g. the ticket-availability colours on
  the `/plan` grid), fetch the official site's CSS with `curl` through the agent
  proxy and read the palette out of it. `WebFetch` returns rendered text without
  the CSS, and headless Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy to reach an external
  host — `curl` is the one path that works for off-box assets.

## The live site is reachable — check real state at `*.edfringenow.com`, allowing for CDN lag

The environment's egress policy allows `*.edfringenow.com`, the live site's own
domain. So a question about what the deployed site actually serves — is the new
field in `data/shows.json`? did the deploy land? — is answerable directly, with
`curl https://www.edfringenow.com/…` through the agent proxy, rather than by
reasoning from the working tree. General egress is still closed: everything
*except* the allowed domain fails the same way, so this is a single-domain
window, not open internet.

Two caveats before you trust what comes back:

- **The response is CDN-cached, so a fresh push may not be visible yet.** A
  200 with stale content is not evidence the deploy failed — re-check after a
  delay, and never conclude "the change didn't ship" from one read taken
  seconds after the push.
- **Confirm the allowance is live in *your* session before relying on it.** The
  policy is per-environment and a session can be running under an older one; on
  2026-08-07 a probe of both `www.edfringenow.com` and the apex returned
  `curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403`. A 403 at CONNECT is a policy
  denial, not a site outage — `curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status"`
  lists the recent rejections and confirms which it is. When it's denied, say so
  and fall back to the repo, rather than reporting the live site as down.

As with the off-box CSS fetch above, `curl` is the working path: headless
Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy, and `WebFetch` returns rendered text rather
than the raw JSON or asset you usually want here.

## Watching a workflow or scheduler run — ask the MCP Actions tools, never poll with `curl`

A run's state comes from `mcp__github__actions_get` / `mcp__github__actions_list`.
Do **not** poll `https://api.github.com/…` from the shell. `gh` is not installed
here, and shell egress to the API is a per-environment policy that has been
*denied* mid-session — and a denied `CONNECT` returns a proxy error body rather
than JSON, so an `until`-loop testing `.status == "completed"` neither
terminates nor says why. Both sessions that reached for it on 2026-08-07 lost
the poll silently: #249 burned two round-trips on a `curl` that "never actually
worked" before the MCP call answered in 5s, and #251 backgrounded an
`until curl …; sleep 15; done`, abandoned it, and fell back to a blind
`sleep 90` — for a run `actions_get` reported *already complete* five seconds
later. The orphaned sleep then fired two `task-notification`s that had to be
explained away to the owner.

So: ask the MCP tool, and if the run is still going ask it again. Never a blind
fixed sleep, and never a shell poll.

## The site is two front-ends — cross-page behaviour goes in `shared/`

The Now page (`index.html` + `js/app.js`) and the planner (`plan/` + `plan/plan.js`)
are separate front-ends, and `plan/lib/` is the planner's own engine, not a common
library. But both are now ES modules, so **anything that must behave the same on
both pages belongs in `shared/`** and is imported by each — never copy-pasted.
Both pages spell the import the same way (`../shared/geo.js` resolves to
`/shared/geo.js` from either), so moving a value there is a small change.

What is still genuinely twinned (untangled the same way when next touched): the
header `debug v<version>` pill, the Now/Plan nav, and the haversine in
`plan/lib/travel.js` that was ported from `js/app.js`.

A shared module needs **no** `package.json` to mark it as ESM: the pinned Node 22
detects module syntax in a `.js` file by itself, with no warning and no flag, so
`node --check` and the test suite both handle it. `plan/package.json` predates
that detection and its stated reason (silencing a module-detection warning) no
longer applies; it is harmless, so it stays, but do not copy it as a pattern —
the `edfringe-no-stray-package-json` check flags any other one.
`.js` and `.mjs` are both served as `text/javascript` by `python3 -m http.server`,
so the extension is a style choice — use `.js`, matching `plan/lib/`.

A new top-level source dir must be added to `scripts/verify.sh`'s `git ls-files`
list, or nothing in it is ever parse-checked — the `edfringe-verify-sh-covers-source-dirs`
check catches an omission. Note that `git ls-files` only sees *tracked* files, so
a new file silently sits outside the syntax sweep until it is committed — the
"checked N files" count is not evidence your new file was among them.

## `.claudinite/shared/` is generated output — never hand-resolve its conflicts, always take the fresher version

## A pack rule or check encodes a *work procedure*, never product behaviour

Rules and checks in `.claudinite/local/packs/` are about **how work is done here**
— the gate that must stay wired, the tool that must be launched a certain way, the
files that must move together. **Product behaviour is not a rule.** What the site
does — which ticket statuses count as unavailable, what the Now page shows, how
far "walkable" reaches — is a **requirement**, and it belongs in the requirements
spec (`product/requirements.md`, the `executable-requirements` pack) and its
tests, never in a pack's `rules`.

The trap is that product behaviour reads exactly like a good check candidate: it
is deterministic, statically detectable, and genuinely worth enforcing, so a
prose-to-checks sweep will happily convert it. The 2026-07-30 sweep did: it turned
the `ticketStatus`-not-`soldOut` rule into an `edfringe-ticket-status-unavailable`
check, with a clean scoped parse and a see-it-fail proof against mutated real repo
content — a well-built check of the wrong kind, which the owner rejected on sight
("Rules shouldn't be about product requirements, only work procedures"). The
sibling conversion in the same PR, `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` ("the
offline self-test must stay wired into `verify.sh`"), was the right kind and
stayed.

Apply the test **before** writing the check, since the build quality of the check
tells you nothing about whether it belongs: *if the product changed its mind
tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* If yes it is a requirement — a red check
would then be reporting a product decision as a process violation, and the
requirements spec is where that decision is already supposed to live. If instead
it would still hold because it describes how we work regardless of what the
product does, it is a rule. Prose in a `RULES.md` gets the same test: the
`ticketStatus` paragraph in the `edfringe-data` pack is background a scraper
editor needs, not a rule, and it is not convertible.
===PACKMJS===
import testGlobsInStep from './test-globs-in-step.mjs';
import verifyShSourceDirs from './verify-sh-source-dirs.mjs';
import noStrayPackageJson from './no-stray-package-json.mjs';

// EdFringeNow's own local pack: project-specific working rules captured in this
// repo, layered on the shared Claudinite canon. Declaration-authoritative (no
// structural fingerprint). Its RULES.md is injected wherever this pack is declared,
// and its checks run against the tree.
export default {
  id: 'edfringe',
  ruleRoutingGuidance: {
    belongs: "EdFringeNow's own working rules — its build steps, shell scripts, and repo layout conventions",
    excludes: 'the edfringe.com scrape and the data layer it produces — those are edfringe-data',
  },
  detect: null,
  marker: null,
  prose: 'RULES.md',
  worldRules: [testGlobsInStep, verifyShSourceDirs, noStrayPackageJson],
};

Fix show times landing an hour early: the API's dateTime is UTC (#274)
Every show on the site was listed an hour before it actually starts. The
data said so itself: the "7am Oboe Rave" sat at 06:00, "Jokes At Noon" at
11:00, "Four O'Clock Afternoon Blues" at 15:00, and Shakespeare for
Breakfast — a 10am institution — at 09:00.

The listing API stamps performances in real UTC
("2026-08-06T11:45:00.000Z"), but normalize.py sliced the digits straight
out of the string on the belief that they were already Edinburgh
wall-clock. August is BST, so the whole catalogue shifted back an hour.

Convert once, at the edge. `normalize.local_date_start` is now the
pipeline's only time-zone crossing; refresh_ticket_status and fetch_prices
share it so a performance is keyed by the same local date and start
everywhere. Everything written downstream — day files, availability
sidecar, catalogue — is Edinburgh wall-clock, and no code after this point
touches a zone.

The committed snapshot was rebuilt through the same conversion: all 60,115
performances shifted, then every derived artifact regenerated from the
master. Two late performances on 31 Aug cross into 1 Sep and so fall
outside the August day files, the same way the July preview dates already
do; both remain in the master and the planner's catalogue.

The Now page's clock moves onto the festival's zone to match. Show times
are Edinburgh wall-clock, so the "now" they are measured against is read
in Edinburgh too (js/clock.js festivalNow / festivalDate) rather than off
the device — otherwise a visitor planning from another zone reintroduces
exactly the drift this commit removes. In the UK nothing changes.

Closes #275

===5455fd6 Name the mixed scheduling conflict instead of a flat "Can't fit" (#271)
A show shut out by a mix of controls — some performances hitting the
lunch break, the rest running past the day end — used to get the muted
"Can't fit" verdict, even though placementDiagnostics knew exactly which
settings were responsible. Now the mix gets its own amber conflict pill
("Lunch + late"), whose hover card names each culprit in the user's own
numbers and whose click scrolls to and flashes every setting responsible.

A show blocked only by *pairs* of settings at once (no single relaxation
frees a performance) gets the same treatment under an "Hours + meals"
label, so "Can't fit" is now reserved for the true clash/cap case.

Closes #272

The disc sat at the top of the block, reading as a bullet on the first
line of the title. Anchoring it to the block's midpoint centres it on the
accent rule in both axes, so it marks the whole show block.

===33a4eb8 Put the conflict triangle on the meal band, restore the status labels (#266)
The board's meal bands carried an orange "(excludes N shows)" pill while the
grid's status column had been reduced to a bare red triangle — the two halves
of the same verdict spoke in different dialects, and the column that has the
room to explain itself was the one that had gone silent.

The band's pill becomes the same red triangle the conflicts use, hovered for
the excluded list exactly as before; the status column gets its label back
beside the mark ("▲ Lunch conflict"), which is what makes the triangle on the
band legible in the first place.

Closes #267

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
===cc7de0a Move the board's chrome into the grid's own corners (#263)
The board header was a row of its own above the calendar carrying the count
line, Clear and the legend toggle. Its three parts now sit where each one
belongs, and the row is gone:

- Clear moves into the grid's top-left corner, over the show names it throws
  away. The corner reserves the armed question's two-line height, so arming
  the button shifts nothing.
- The count line moves up to the page title's line, right-aligned — it is the
  page's headline number.
- The legend toggle moves to the grid's top-right corner, above the Status
  column it keys.

The key itself becomes a popup over the grid's top-right corner rather than a
column beside it: opening and closing it no longer resizes the calendar under
the pointer. Being transient, it opens closed on every load and closes on a
click elsewhere or Escape, so its stored open/closed preference is gone.

Both corners live inside the calendar's fixed-height scroll box, so dropping
the header row shortens the card by the same amount in both the empty and the
populated state — the search bar below it stays put when the first show lands.

Closes #264

===430f448 Cache each data file for as long as its contents last (#252)
* Cache each data file for as long as its contents last

The site has no server it controls — GitHub Pages sets its own
Cache-Control with no way to vary it per file — so the freshness policy
lives on the client, in the new shared/data-cache.js. Both pages now use
it, with a TTL per file rather than a single blanket one.

The catalogue could only earn a long TTL by giving up the one thing in it
that changes hourly. So per-performance ticket status moves out of
shows.min.json into its own sidecar, availability.min.json — self-contained
(its own status list, indexing into nothing) so the hourly refresh can
rewrite it alone. The catalogue is now regenerated byte-for-byte identically
over an unchanged festival, which is what makes holding it for days safe.

  shows.min.json          4 days   948 KB gz, nothing in it moves
  availability.min.json   1 day    149 KB gz, moves hourly
  venues.json             1 day    small; the cached catalogue indexes into it
  days/2026-08-DD.json    1 day    carries ticket status
  descriptions.min.json   7 days   unchanged

Fixes #249, whose two gaps this split resolves at the root:

  * refresh_ticket_status.py wrote only data/days/*.json, which the planner
    has never loaded — every hourly commit changed nothing it could see. It
    now writes statuses through the master and regenerates every derived
    file from it, so one source of truth feeds all of them.
  * It stopped at today, leaving every future date frozen at the last manual
    full scrape. It now covers today through the end of the run; one listing
    pass already returned those performances, so the wider window is free.

Two invariants hold the caching up, both silent if broken, both now tested:
the venues.json lookup lists are append-only (extend_lookup), since a
four-day-old catalogue is decoded against a venues.json fetched today; and
shows.min.json carries nothing day-varying, asserted per wire performance.

Also fixes the hydrate round-trip test, red on main: it expected the
master's `description` back from the catalogue, which deliberately leaves it
to descriptions.min.json. It now strips the field and asserts it survives in
that sidecar instead, so "moved" can't become "lost".
